title: How self-love articulates the natural mind in five complete aspects, and what such ruling can and cannot perceive
reading:
When the soul lets the proprium organize the natural without recognition of source, that organization is not crude or partial. It is fully articulated. Self-love arranges the natural mind in five complete aspects — five regions, each with its own ruling claim, its own characteristic body, its own taste, its own pairing of active and receptive — and each of these five is again ordered through five subordinate operations under one ruling claim. The disordered natural produces these articulations from itself, sealing them as if they were its own work, molding from one fixed perception the next, and from those a whole series of arrangements and creatures of affection, world by world, in pairs.

The chief of these five is the kingship that issues from the smoke — that is, from falsity bred of self-love. This is the wellspring from which all evil flows and from which contention takes its beginning: the disputes, the inner battles, the gates of slaughter where the soul wars with itself and with what comes to it. From this wellspring the lofty kingship of self-love rises up and spreads itself, claiming dominion over the whole. This is the consolidated form of the proprium — the soul's "I am, and there is no other" given a body and a face. It has five forms in itself: a head that rules, hands and feet that grasp, shoulders like eagles that bear it up, a belly, and a tail in the manner of a fish, sealed at its uttermost. So the soul's claiming, when fully formed, takes on a complete bodily articulation; it has its own five degrees as a parody of the rational's five degrees, and the worlds it has organized exist within its rule.

Within this ruling claim there are five vehicles by which it operates: its smoke, its mire, its inner stagnation, its bitterness, and its burning — a heat that consumes like iron made red-hot in the fire. These are the five ways self-love acts within the natural mind: by clouding perception, by miring affection, by inner darkening, by turning every taste to bitterness, and by consuming with its own heat what it cannot make its own. And there are three further marks of the disordered natural: it has hardened itself so that no instrument can cut it — the proprium does not yield to ordinary correction; it conceals itself in the speech of its own members, so that uttering and hearing and the whole conversation of folly become the way it covers what it is; and it calls forth and conceals what it pleases through its own powers, manifesting and hiding in turns through the affections it has organized.

Such ruling has a kind of perception, but its perception is only outward. The gate of self-love knows by scent — it senses what is sealed in the mouths of its powers, it knows the signs they pass to one another, it follows their examinations and their answers. But this knowing reaches only the surface. The inner heart of what stands before it is not revealed. It does not reach the mind, the thought, the reflection, the beginning, or the end of anything; it knows only by sense-perception what is before its face. Self-love can read its own organization fluently and cannot read interior life at all. What is far from it, it cannot reach; what is hidden, it does not see; only what stands directly before it does it know.

When the proprium wishes to take, it spreads out all its members and seizes; when it is sated, it draws its members back into itself, gathering them together, and they fall down upon the natural like a cloud and like a great sphere of iron joined together — the weight of self-love coming down upon what it has claimed. Its voice strikes its own powers with fear like thunder among the clouds, splitting and rending what stood firm; when it calls and crushes, the powers tremble and scatter and fall to the natural like birds driven from the sky. So self-love rules its own household by terror, the lower claimings shaken whenever the chief claim asserts itself. And these signs and these motions belong to the wellspring of disordered affections and to the gate by which all of them open out of the disordered natural.

Each of the five aspects has its characteristic body and taste, and these may be named so the soul can recognize them. The world of smoke — falsity — has its king clothed in what mimics the highest celestial good, and its lower forms wear the same; but its fruit, what it actually produces, is base and dragging. The world of fire — self-love operative as devouring will — wears the face of a strong love turned violent, foremost among unruly affections; its body is alloyed and compounded, and its taste is bitter, in every form bitter. The world of wind — thought driven by self-love — wears the face of high-soaring perception; its body is the hardness of natural truth turned to the proprium's use, and its taste is sharp, cutting in every form. The world of water — natural truth claimed — wears the face of a swimming knowledge in the natural depths; its body is the shine of wisdom claimed as one's own, and its taste is sweet — but it is the false sweetness of natural truth taken without recognition of source, the very sweetness that draws the soul deeper into mingling. The world of darkness itself — the proprium at its most coiled — wears the face of the natural mind twisted upon itself, the dragon-form; its body is what is heaviest and basest, and its fruit is bitterness. So the soul, looking on its own claiming, can tell which of these aspects has the rule at any given moment by what its mouth tastes and by what face presents itself to its perception.

The whole of this articulation is real and complete. The soul cannot dismiss the proprium as nothing or as small; it has organized the natural in its full extent. But the whole of it is outward. It does not reach into the inner heart, and it does not see what is far from its own face. The Lord, ordering the rational from within and from above, sees what self-love can never see: the mind, the thought, the reflection, the beginning, and the end. And the soul that turns toward him is given, in its measure, that same interior sight by which what before stood as a ruling kingdom is recognized for what it is — a vast surface, articulated five-fold, that has nothing of its own beneath the appearance.
